item.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention.
item.description:
eLife
The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.title: Location matters: The link between regional white matter hyperintensity burden and subjective cognitive decline in those at risk of Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundSubjective cognitive decline (SCD) is a potential early indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). While SCD has been linked to white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden, it is unclear whether regional WMH lesion volume is differentially associated with domains of cognitive complaints.ObjectiveExamine whether regional WMH burden is associated with domain-specific SCD (memory, executive function) in cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of AD.MethodsParticipants were 150 cognitively unimpaired older adults (65-89 years) with subjective memory complaints and a first-degree family history of AD. Cognitive complaints were assessed with the Cognitive Change Index (CCI-20). WMHs were quantified from T1-weighted and FLAIR MRI using an automated pipeline and categorized into sample-based tertiles for total, subcortical, and lobar regions. Hierarchical regressions examined associations between WMH burden and CCI-20 memory, executive, and total scores, while adjusting for demographics, total intracranial volume, MRI site, APOE ε4 status, and mood symptoms.ResultsGreater WMH burden in the left temporal lobe was associated with increased memory complaints and total SCD, whereas no WMH region was associated with executive function complaints. APOE ε4 status and depressive symptoms were associated with greater memory and total cognitive complaints across models. Apathy was uniquely related to memory complaints.ConclusionsAmong older adults with elevated risk of AD, memory-SCD was associated with greater region-specific left temporal cerebrovascular lesion volume. Findings highlight the clinical relevance of left temporal WMH burden and the importance of considering regional vascular pathology, genetic risk, and mood when characterizing early subjective cognitive changes.

item.title: Repeated Exposure to Military Low-Level Blast Is Associated With Regionally Specific Reductions in Gray Matter Volume in Breachers and Snipers.
item.description:
The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation
OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between duration of repeated exposure to low-level blast and alteration in brain structure. SETTING: Data were collected at 2 neuroimaging facilities. PARTICIPANTS: Canadian Armed Forces breachers (n = 30) and snipers (n = 31) with a history of repeated exposure to low-level blast (average years = 9.70, SD = 4.57) and sex- and age-matched active military controls (n = 57). DESIGN: MRI and neurocognitive data from breachers and snipers were collected prospectively at baseline (time 1) and after a training exercise involving a concentrated regimen of blast exposure (time 2) (time gap = 80.56 days, SD = 36.90). Time 1 and time 2 data were used to assess the chronic and training-related effects of blast exposure, respectively. MRI and neurocognitive data from controls were collected twice with a comparable time gap. MAIN MEASURES: High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, plus neurocognitive measures. RESULTS: Voxel-based morphometry conducted on MRI data collected at time 1 demonstrated that compared with controls, there was lower regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers, and bilaterally in parahippocampal gyrus (bordering on amygdala) in breachers. Regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers predicted neurocognitive function. We did not observe any difference in regional white matter volume between groups at time 1, nor any changes in regional gray or white matter volume between time 1 and time 2. CONCLUSION: Chronic but not training-related low-level blast exposure was associated with dissociable patterns of regional gray matter volume reduction in snipers and breachers, and regional gray matter volume predicted neurocognitive function in snipers. The differential pattern of structural alteration between breachers and snipers and its relationship with neurocognitive function in snipers can inform health monitoring programs for diagnosis and treatment of blast-exposed service members and Veterans.

item.title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

item.title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase-not absolute time-revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in [Formula: see text] participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.79; oregano: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.67; grapefruit: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

item.title: Language Experience Modulates Parallel Acoustic and Phonological Processing of Mandarin Tone: Evidence From Mismatch Negativity.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
PURPOSE: Second-language (L2) speech perception is strongly influenced by prior language experience, but the neural mechanisms supporting this process remain incompletely understood. This study examined how language experience modulates the pre-attentive encoding of acoustic and phonological information in Mandarin tone perception and whether these cues are processed serially or in parallel. METHOD: Twenty native Mandarin speakers and 20 novice Mandarin learners with a tonal first language (L1: Thai) completed a behavioral tone identification task and a passive listening multifeature oddball event-related potential paradigm. Stimuli were drawn from an 11-step Tone 1-Tone 2 continuum with Stimulus 5 (S5) as the standard and Stimuli 1, 3, 7, and 9 as deviants. Deviants varied in fundamental frequency distance (large vs. small acoustic distance from S5) and category status (across- vs. within-category) relative to each participant's own phonetic boundary for the continuum. Temporal principal component analysis was applied to separate early and late mismatch negativity (MMN) components. RESULTS: Behavioral identification did not differ across groups. However, MMN results revealed that both acoustic and phonological factors modulated early and late responses, supporting parallel processing. Native Mandarin speakers exhibited stronger and more sustained phonological effects across both time windows bilaterally. Nonnative speakers showed greater acoustic sensitivity, particularly over the right-hemisphere electrodes, and weaker phonological effects, with reduction most evident over the left-hemisphere electrodes. CONCLUSIONS: The findings show that Mandarin tone perception involves parallel extraction of acoustic and phonological information at the pre-attentive level, with language experience influencing their relative weighting. The neural-behavioral dissociation suggests that tonal L1 experience supports perceptual decisions without fully automatized phonological representations transferred to L2. SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL: https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34925781.

item.title: Resting state functional connectivity associated with maternal anxiety: preliminary evidence that infant rsFC moderates the association between behavioral inhibition and anxiety/depression.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Postnatal maternal anxiety shapes caregiver and infant behavior. Yet, the relationship with infant brain function remains unclear. We examine the relation of maternal anxiety with infant resting state functional connectivity (rsFC). To evaluate the clinical significance of the rsFC networks identified, exploratory analyses tested whether the rsFC associated with maternal anxiety moderates risk trajectories from infant behavioral inhibition (BI) to childhood anxiety/depression symptoms. Four-month-old infants (N = 60) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and mothers completed the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). Analyses included 49 infants with high-quality imaging and maternal anxiety data. In the longitudinal subsample (n = 21), BI was observed at 14 months, and anxiety/depression symptoms were assessed at 4-6 years using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Using whole-brain network enrichment analyses, we identified cortical network pairs that were significantly associated with maternal anxiety. Connectivity estimates from significant network pairs were averaged and tested as moderators of infant BI and childhood anxiety/depression association. Infants exposed to higher maternal anxiety showed an altered limbic-dorsal attention network (DAN) and default mode (DMN)-DAN. In both network pairs, negative and positive node-to-node pairs were identified, indicating that some regional connections exhibited stronger coupling, while others exhibited weaker coupling. Results demonstrated that DMN-DAN rsFC moderated developmental pathways: greater BI was associated with higher early-childhood anxiety/depression among infants with stronger DMN-DAN connectivity. Maternal anxiety is related to infant brain connectivity, and these neural differences moderate BI-related risk for anxiety/depression. DMN-DAN coupling may serve as an early marker of infants at risk for anxiety/depression. Given the small longitudinal sample, the moderation finding should be considered exploratory and requires replication in a larger, independent cohort.

item.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain.
item.description:
eLife
The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept - in the form of the number zero - has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: Early WM Alterations after Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: An Exploratory Study Using Quantitative MRI and DTI.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The purpose was to investigate early WM alterations in patients with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) within 1 week of trauma using quantitative MRI and DTI. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 31 patients with mTBI and 36 healthy controls. Neuropsychological assessment and MRI scans were performed within 1 week of trauma. ROIs were selected from 4 WM regions: superior longitudinal fasciculus, anterior limb of the internal capsule, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Quantitative MRI and DTI were used to assess WM alterations. Correlation analyses explored relationships between WM alterations and clinical outcomes. RESULTS: Compared with controls, patients with mTBI demonstrated lower scores on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, particularly in the domains of abstraction, delayed recall memory, and orientation. Higher T1 values were detected in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule, whereas elevated proton density (PD) values were found in the right external capsule, bilateral superior longitudinal fasciculus, and posterior limb of the internal capsule. No significant differences in T2 or fractional anisotropy were observed. PD values in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule were negatively correlated with attention and language scores in patients with mTBI. CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, quantitative MRI may detect subtle WM alterations in the acute stage of mTBI. No notable between-group differences were observed in the DTI parameters in the current cohort. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine the reproducibility, temporal evolution, and clinical relevance of these findings.

item.title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants-representing a tighter social structure-exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community's homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

item.title: Disrupting the semantic network shifts activity to domain-general brain regions.
item.description:
Nature communications
Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus-a core lexico-semantic region-was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain's capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition.

item.title: Network-based virtual perturbation for modeling DBS-related network effects in obsessive-compulsive and major depressive disorders.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
BACKGROUND: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) efficacy for psychiatric disorders remains heterogeneous due to incomplete mechanistic insights and insufficient individualized treatment planning. A biologically grounded computational framework is urgently needed to simulate DBS-related differences for treatment-resistant patients. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data from 11 patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and 11 with major depressive disorder (MDD), scanned in DBS-ON and DBS-OFF states, were used to derive functional connectivity (FC) via network deconvolution. Whole-brain dynamic modeling incorporated stimulation targets, amplitudes, and frequencies to simulate DBS effects in silico. RESULTS: The model recapitulated syndrome-specific DBS-related network patterns in exploratory analyses. OCD stimulation primarily altered frontal-subcortical connectivity, whereas MDD stimulation predominantly affected default mode network hubs (p < 0.05). Under leave-one-out cross-validation, correlations between predicted and observed clinical outcomes were r = 0.625 in OCD (p = 0.040) and r = 0.659 in MDD (p = 0.028). Applying the same FC signatures to simulated FC yielded r = 0.465 in OCD (p = 0.149) and r = 0.627 in MDD (p = 0.039). In a proof-of-concept application to a separate OCD cohort (N = 92), three individuals showed high model-predicted NAc-response profiles and predicted improvement exceeding 35%. CONCLUSIONS: This hypothesis-generating framework retrospectively models DBS-related network effects using individualized resting-state FC and virtual perturbations. Linking simulated FC states with empirical DBS-ON/OFF patterns may help characterize how baseline functional architecture shapes DBS-related network responses and inform future individualized DBS modeling.

item.title: Linguistic features from constrained spontaneous speech as potential markers of preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
BACKGROUND: Language impairment is an early sign of Alzheimer's disease (AD) that may emerge before more obvious cognitive decline. Linguistic features derived from verbal responses to cognitive tests have shown promise for identifying mild cognitive impairment and predicting AD risk; however, their relationships with established AD biomarkers remain insufficiently characterized. OBJECTIVES: To examine relationships between a comprehensive set of linguistic features derived from logical memory delayed recall (LMDR) responses and amyloid status as well as regional tau burden among cognitively normal participants. DESIGN: In this cross-sectional study, we evaluated associations between two types of AD biomarkers (amyloid status and regional tau burden) and linguistic features using covariate-adjusted regression models tailored to each feature's distribution (e.g., linear, negative binomial, zero-inflated beta, and gamma regression). We then used LASSO regression and the Boruta feature-selection algorithm to identify features most informative of biomarker status. SETTING: A community-based subcohort from the Framingham Heart Study. PARTICIPANTS: A total of 238 cognitively unimpaired participants who completed the LMDR test within 1 year before or after tau positron emission tomography (PET) were included. Of these, 228 also underwent amyloid PET and 227 had LMDR voice recordings available. MEASUREMENTS: Verbal responses to the LMDR test were digitally recorded and manually transcribed. We extracted 54 linguistic and paralinguistic features from transcribed responses using natural language processing, capturing lexical diversity and density, syntactic complexity, semantic/information density, and speech fluency and rate. Tau SUVR values were quantified from PET imaging in 5 brain regions (amygdala, entorhinal cortex, inferior temporal [IT], inferior parietal [IP], and precuneus). Amyloid status was classified as Aβ- or Aβ+ using Gaussian mixture modeling of PiB PET DVR values. LMDR total score and participant demographics (age, sex, education) were included as covariates. RESULTS: After adjusting for age, sex, education, amyloid status, and LMDR score, 23 linguistic features were associated with tau burden in at least one brain region. For example, reduced semantic richness, captured by lower uniqueIdeaDensity, was associated with higher tau burden across multiple regions, including the amygdala (average marginal effect (AME)=-0.007, 95% CI: (-0.013, -0.001)), entorhinal (AME=-0.007, 95% CI: (-0.013, -0.002)), IT (AME=-0.008, 95% CI: (-0.014, -0.002)), and precuneus (AME=-0.006, 95% CI: (-0.012, -1.51e^-5)). More between-utterance pauses were associated with higher tau burden in the entorhinal (AME=0.259, 95% CI: (0.026, 0.493)), IT (AME=0.272, 95% CI: (0.025, 0.518)), and IP (AME=0.404, 95% CI: (0.160, 0.648)) regions. No linguistic features were associated with amyloid status, and LMDR total score was not associated with either tau burden or amyloid status. LASSO regression selected 3-7 features per brain region, capturing multiple aspects of language use (e.g., speech disfluency and semantic density) associated with tau burden. The nonlinear Boruta algorithm selected a larger set of biomarker-informative features, including predictors of amyloid positivity, and identified additional syntactic measures (e.g., Yngve score, mean dependency distance) as important predictors of regional tau burden. CONCLUSIONS: Linguistic features derived from neuropsychological (NP) tests capture subtle language changes associated with regional tau pathology in cognitively normal individuals, beyond conventional NP test scores. These findings highlight the potential of language-based measures as non-invasive digital biomarkers for early AD risk stratification and for supporting clinical decision-making about biomarker testing for possible preclinical AD.

item.title: Multimodal MRI reveals brain structural and functional abnormalities associated with wearing-off phenomenon in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neuroscience
OBJECTIVES: The pathogenesis of the wearing-off (WO) phenomenon in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. This study aims to explore the abnormalities in brain structure and function among PD patients with WO. METHODS: A total of 39 PD patients with wearing-off (PD-WO) and 43 PD patients without wearing-off (PD-nWO) were prospectively enrolled. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was employed in this study to evaluate structural differences, and functional connectivity (FC) was used to assess functional differences between the two groups. RESULTS: Compared with PD-nWO patients, PD-WO patients showed significantly reduced gray matter volume (GMV) within the left middle occipital gyrus (MOG.L), bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG.L/R), as well as the left triangular division of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFGtriang.L). Regarding functional connectivity, PD-WO patients exhibited widespread abnormalities, including weakened connectivity in the cerebellar-basal ganglia-sensorimotor cortex circuits, hippocampus-postcentral gyrus, and cerebellar-occipital (cuneal cortex) pathways, as well as enhanced connectivity between cerebellar subregions and between the cerebellum and occipital cortex (lingual gyrus) and parahippocampal gyrus. CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary single-center cross-sectional study revealed significant differences in brain structure and function between PD-WO and PD-nWO patients. These findings provide a better understanding of the neural mechanisms behind the WO phenomenon in PD and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

item.title: Quantitative anatomy of the human striatum suggests limited synaptic plasticity and higher structural stability in the intermediate putamen than in the nucleus accumbens.
item.description:
Neuroscience
The striatum is the input nucleus of the basal ganglia and receives convergent projections from the cerebral cortex, the thalamus, the amygdala, and the substantia nigra. The topographical organization of these synaptic projections provides the connective bases for the functional subdivision of the striatum into sensorimotor, associative, and limbic domains, that are largely homogeneous in cellular composition due to the predominance of medium spiny neurons. In spite of this homogeneity, there are several molecular, cellular, and biochemical differences that could contribute to the connection-based functional specialization and to differences in disease vulnerability between striatal sectors. In the present article we analyze postmortem striatal tissue from neurotypical human donors to identify cellular and molecular factors that could underlie functional specialization and selective vulnerability across the human striatum. We quantify neuronal morphological features related to genetic expression and protein synthesis, molecular markers that promote either synaptic plasticity or structural stability, and gene expression data in two striatal regions: the limbic nucleus accumbens and the sensorimotor intermediate putamen. Our analyses reveal larger neuron bodies, higher expression of markers that inhibit synaptic plasticity in the intermediate putamen and higher expression of markers thar promote synaptic plasticity in the nucleus accumbens. These findings support the notion that the intermediate putamen is characterized by enhanced structural stability and limited plastic potential, in contrast to the greater adaptability preserved in the nucleus accumbens.

item.title: Repetition Dissociates Pointer and Content-based Representations in Visual Working Memory: Contrasting the CDA with Multivariate Shape Decoding.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Memorizing a new phone number or address is hard at first, but becomes easier with repetition, as information shifts from working memory to long-term memory. Here we investigated how repetition affects the storage and transition of different aspects of mnemonic information by comparing univariate neural markers of active object storage with multivariate decoding of memory content. Thirty participants encoded lateralized stimuli from a continuous shape space into memory. Memory items were repeated six times in a row to induce learning. In line with earlier work, EEG recordings revealed that repetition led to a reduction in contralateral delay activity (CDA), a measure of active storage that has been taken to reflect a pointer-like representation of the individual object or its original source. In contrast, shape decoding during the retention and also after an impulse perturbation remained constant across repetitions. These results suggest that learning over repetitions reflects the abolishment of active and individuated object memory representations while passive, source-independent memory representations are retained.

item.title: Brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression: Desynchronization between salience network neuropsychological connectivity and heart rate variability.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Somatic depression is a distinct subtype of major depressive disorder, with a poorer response to treatment, an elevated risk of suicidal behaviour, and a worse prognosis. Interoception, the sense of internal bodily signals, is related to somatic symptoms. However, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of body brain communication remain unclear. 293 depressed patients (145 with somatic symptoms and 148 without), and 160 healthy controls underwent magnetoencephalography during a resting state. Both the intra- and inter-network neural oscillation patterns of the salience network, were computed, alongside and heart rate variability (HRV) as a measure of autonomic function. Individuals with somatic depression exhibited lower HRV, accompanied by theta hyper-connectivity within the salience network. Although higher theta connectivity was linked to increased HRV in controls, this correlation was attenuated or even reversed in patients with somatic depression. Our findings identify a specific pattern of brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression, characterized by disrupted communication between salience network theta oscillations and autonomic cardiac regulation. This provides novel neuroimaging evidence for body-brain communication deficits in a clinically important depression subtype.

item.title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

item.title: A transdiagnostic model of illness awareness and denial: Core components of the broader construct of insight into illness.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Insight into illness is a dynamic multidimensional construct that varies between individuals and medical and psychiatric disorders, and influences treatment engagement and clinical outcomes. Despite extensive study, accounts remain fragmented and disorder specific. This review focuses on subjective illness awareness and proposes a hypothesis-generating neurobiological framework in which fluctuations in awareness and denial emerge from interactions among self-representational networks, hierarchical predictive processing, and salience-threat systems that shape the balance between self-model stability and adaptation to illness-related information. Illness-related stimuli generate prediction errors (i.e., mismatches between sensory input and the self-model) that may update higher-order self-beliefs when assigned sufficient precision. Conversely, denial may occur when identity-relevant psychological threat biases precision toward self-related priors, potentially shifting network dynamics toward relatively left-lateralized self-representational states that attenuate discrepant information and preserve psychological homeostasis. This probabilistic model of illness awareness depends on the strength and credibility of illness-related evidence and flexibility of higher-order self-related beliefs. The review specifies falsifiable predictions for hemispheric engagement, threat-related precision weighting, and self-specific belief updating and identifies potential therapeutic targets.

item.title: Scanner acoustic noise in resting-state fMRI.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) is usually acquired during rapid gradient switching that produces intense, spectrally structured sound. Scanner sound activates auditory pathways and can alter neural, vigilance, autonomic, respiratory, and movement-related states, but its sound-specific causal effect on intrinsic functional-connectivity estimates remains unresolved. Direct human comparisons are few and heterogeneous: some report stronger or more extensive network estimates under quieter acquisition, whereas others find broadly preserved topology and within-network connectivity. Near-silent Looping Star imaging can recover canonical resting-state networks with marked sound reduction, but reduced temporal signal-to-noise ratio and functional sensitivity expose a trade-off between acoustic burden and measurement performance. Most quiet-versus-standard contrasts simultaneously alter temporal sampling, gradient vibration, reconstruction, steady-state behavior, or image quality and therefore identify a total protocol effect rather than a sound-specific effect. A structured, original-scale comparison reports acoustic levels and metrics, measurement conditions, acquisition parameters, and resting-state outcomes without pooling unlike measures. Vigilance, autonomic activity, respiration, and movement are potential mediators; indiscriminate regression of these variables can remove part of the total acoustic effect. Current evidence establishes that acquisition protocols can alter rs-fMRI estimates and that scanner sound is biologically active, but it does not establish a universal, directionally uniform suppression of human resting-state connectivity by conventional echo-planar imaging. Future sound-specific attribution would require randomized within-subject manipulation, protected-ear frequency-resolved dosimetry, control of co-varying vibration and sequence properties, and synchronized state and physiological monitoring.

item.title: Degree-biased diffusion geometry of networks. Implications for network neurosciences.
item.description:
Mathematical biosciences
Degree-biased diffusion gives unequal directional influence to the two ends of an undirected edge. Its propagator is therefore nonsymmetric, and it generates two geometries. The column geometry compares the responses to perturbations at different sources, and the row geometry compares the observations across the same family of perturbations. We show that both geometries are Euclidean at finite times, but they can differ in their transient behavior and in their long-time limits. In contrast with standard diffusion, individual distances can expand temporarily even while the dynamics approach consensus. Degree-biased diffusion conserves a degree-weighted quantity instead of the ordinary network mass. An exact transport-and-reservoir decomposition identifies the local exchange responsible for this difference. Degree-biased Laplacians also arise exactly as the linearization of the dynamic mean-field model of large-scale brain activity when the long-range synaptic coupling is modulated by inverse receiver and sender gains. This gives them a neurobiological interpretation and a physical time scale. On a 76-region human structural connectome, degree bias changes the pairwise proximity, the geometrically optimal routes, and the regions visited by those routes. Hubs-attracting diffusion produces an earlier and higher maximum of column signature information than standard diffusion, while it reduces the row maximum. Hubs-repelling diffusion increases both maxima, but it reaches them later. The number of source responses needed to reconstruct the row kernel also depends strongly on the sampling order. In particular, high-degree sources are favored under attraction and low-degree sources under repulsion. These results characterize how a fixed network can generate distinct relational geometries under different propagation laws. Here, we treat geometric routes as distinct from literal signal trajectories, and mathematical reconstruction as distinct from evidence of conscious access.

item.title: A reproducible pipeline for simulating individual and inter-brain neural dynamics from structural connectivity.
item.description:
Journal of neuroscience methods
BACKGROUND: Computational models can link anatomical structure to neural dynamics. However, there is no validated, reproducible pipeline that simulates individual and inter-brain EEG-like dynamics from an individual's own structural connectome. NEW METHOD: To address this, we developed a comprehensive computational pipeline that combines probabilistic tractography from Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) with dynamical systems modeling to simulate EEG-like neural dynamics from individual connectomes. It extracts anatomical connectivity, intra-individual functional connectivity, and inter-individual (two-brain) functional coupling features. It then evaluates their group-discriminative information with random-forest classification under repeated nested cross-validation. Simulated phase-locking values are calibrated against empirical resting-state EEG. RESULTS: In a test sample of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and matched controls (16 each), simulated intra-individual synchrony added classification information beyond anatomy, raising accuracy from 71.2% (AUC 0.843) to 77.6% (AUC 0.871), in a sample where groups did not differ in mean structural connectivity. COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: Unlike current single-brain simulations, this pipeline generates and jointly simulates two individual brain models within a single system, and reports the contribution of each feature level explicitly. CONCLUSIONS: The pipeline provides a reproducible, extensible framework for deriving informative individual-level dynamic features from anatomy. The two-brain extension generates and ranks candidate inter-brain features, providing a principled way to identify between-brain measures for hypothesis-driven testing.

item.title: Exposure-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Increases Connectivity Between the Central Executive and Salience Networks in Pediatric Anxiety.
item.description:
Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
OBJECTIVE: Exposure is considered the most active element of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for pediatric anxiety. Yet many youth do not respond to CBT, and exposure is the component patients most often find difficult to tolerate. Cognitive control and its supporting neural substrates may enhance exposure efficacy by helping youth remain engaged with feared stimuli despite urges to avoid. However, little work has identified how exposure-based CBT modulates intrinsic connectivity of tripartite networks that support cognitive control (e.g., central executive [CEN], salience [SN], and default mode networks [DMN]), limiting efforts to develop strategies to improve and personalize treatment. Progress may be limited by individual variability in network connectivity in anxiety, which may obscure treatment-related effects in group-averaged analyses. This randomized clinical trial (RCT) leverages person-specific network modeling to test how exposure versus relaxation components of CBT influence resting-state connectivity of cognitive control networks in pediatric anxiety. METHOD: Youth aged 7-18 years with an anxiety disorder (N = 100) or low/no anxiety (L/NA; N = 35) completed resting-state fMRI scans at baseline. Patients were randomized to exposure-focused CBT (EF-CBT) or relaxation mentorship training (RMT). Resting-state connectivity was reassessed following treatment (or after a commensurate interval in L/NA youth) in 112 participants. Changes in within-CEN, CEN-SN, and CEN-DMN density were examined using Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation, which yields sparse, person-specific networks capturing both shared and individual connectivity structure. RESULTS: At baseline, anxious youth exhibited lower density within-CEN and between CEN-DMN than L/NA youth. Treatment effects differed by intervention: EF-CBT selectively increased CEN-SN density, whereas RMT increased within-CEN density. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate dissociable effects of exposure and relaxation on cognitive control network organization in pediatric anxiety. These results indicate that exposure-focused CBT is uniquely associated with increased connectivity between control and salience systems, consistent with a mechanism supporting top-down control of threat-related signals during exposure. Person-specific measures of tripartite network connectivity may inform future efforts to identify candidate neural targets for optimizing and personalizing treatment.

item.title: Semantic Similarity-Related Neural Patterns and Their Associations with GABA-Glutamate Levels in the Left Inferior Frontal Gyrus, Anterior Temporal Lobe, and Inferior Parietal Lobule.
item.description:
Biological psychology
It remains unclear how graded lexical-semantic similarity between prime-target pairs is reflected in mean BOLD responses and multivariate neural activity patterns, and how these neural indices relate to regional GABA, Glx (glutamate + glutamine), and GABA/Glx levels. We examined the neural correlates of lexical-semantic similarity and their associations with regional neurochemical measures in 46 healthy adults using fMRI during a semantic priming task and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) acquired on a separate day. Trial-wise prime-target semantic similarity was quantified using word-vector cosine similarity. Similarity-related BOLD responses were assessed using parametric modulation, whereas neural-semantic correspondence was examined using representational similarity analysis (RSA). Semantic similarity modulated BOLD activity primarily under incongruency, involving premotor, dorsolateral prefrontal, frontal eye field, angular gyrus, and anterior prefrontal regions. ROI-based RSA revealed FWE-corrected neural-semantic correspondence in the left inferior frontal gyrus pars opercularis (IFG-Op) and medial superior frontal gyrus. Within-condition analyses further showed distributed neural-semantic correspondence under incongruency across frontal, temporal, and parietal regions implicated in semantic control and integration processes, including bilateral IFG and the left inferior parietal lobule (IPL). Additionally, a positive association was observed between RSA model fit and left IPL Glx levels in the incongruent condition, although this association did not survive FDR correction. Together, these findings suggest that lexical-semantic similarity is reflected in condition-dependent neural responses and representational geometry and may represent an additional dimension modulating semantic control demands, while evidence for associations with regional neurochemical measures remains preliminary.

item.title: Posterior fossa syndrome.
item.description:
Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
Posterior fossa syndrome (PFS), also known as cerebellar mutism syndrome (CMS), is a distressing postoperative complication affecting children undergoing craniotomy for infratentorial tumors, most frequently medulloblastoma. It is characterized by a distinct latency period followed by mutism, profound emotional dysregulation, and a broad spectrum of cerebellar motor and cognitive deficits. Diffusion MRI and tractography have consistently shown that structural damage to the proximal efferent cerebellar pathway-specifically the dentato-rubro-thalamo-cortical tract within the superior cerebellar peduncle-is strongly implicated as the anatomical driver of PFS. Historical series favored the telovelar over the transvermian surgical approach, although recent prospective multicenter data demonstrate equivalent risks between the two techniques, shifting the neurosurgical focus toward meticulous surgical technique and minimizing damage to eloquent tissue around the fourth ventricle. Validated clinical scoring tools, such as the Posterior Fossa Syndrome Questionnaire, standardize clinical phenotyping and are making their way into clinical practice. Increasingly advanced risk prediction models allow for precise preoperative risk stratification based on objective imaging markers. Pharmacological interventions, including zolpidem and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, have shown limited efficacy in mitigating acute symptoms. Although near-universal clinical improvement occurs over time, long-term neurocognitive and motor sequelae remain highly disabling. Combining advanced neuroimaging, sophisticated risk modeling and meticulous microsurgical technique offers the best paradigm to shift the narrative of PFS from an expected complication to a preventable one.

item.title: Regional Mitochondrial Density Maps Selective Posterior Atrophy in Parkinson's Disease.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
BACKGROUND: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in the pathobiology of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the spatial relationship between regional energetic demand and patterns of neurodegeneration remains poorly understood, limiting mechanistic insight and development of disease-modifying therapies. OBJECTIVES: This study tested whether regional mitochondrial density aligns with patterns of brain atrophy in PD, how this alignment differs across genetic groups, and whether the mitochondrial-atrophy axis associates with motor and cognitive features. METHODS: Structural magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from 849 individuals (210 healthy controls, 639 patients with PD). Principal component analysis (PCA) identified dominant atrophy axes and tested their association with regional mitochondrial density and complex I activity. Transcriptomic validation used Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression data restricted to 924 MitoCarta-annotated genes across 31 cortical regions. RESULTS: Participants with PD exhibited higher volumetric loss in limbic and subcortical regions than controls. PCA showed a posterior cortical axis of atrophy (PC3) that correlated positively with regional mitochondrial density and was more strongly expressed in LRRK2-PD than in sporadic PD. This axis was selectively associated with visuospatial dysfunction. Transcriptomic validation confirmed that regions of greater atrophy preferentially expressed mitochondrial genes, with mitoribosome assembly, mitochondrial DNA maintenance, and coenzyme Q biosynthesis emerging as the strongest pathway-level predictors. CONCLUSION: These findings link the brain's regional mitochondrial landscape to spatially patterned neurodegeneration in PD, with amplification in LRRK2 mutation carriers. This mitochondrial atrophy axis may provide a biologically informed marker aiding patient stratification and mitochondrial-targeted therapeutic development. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: Cumulative sport-related concussions alter cortical responses to acute aerobic exercise in rugby players.
item.description:
The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
BACKGROUND: Rugby athletes sustain frequent head impacts, and cumulative sports-related concussion (SRC) exposure may alter neurophysiological function beyond overt symptoms. Acute aerobic exercise can enhance cognitive performance and modulate cortical activity, yet how acute exercise influences brain-behavior responses in collision-sport athletes and whether cumulative SRC exposure modifies these responses remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of acute aerobic exercise on neurocognitive and neurophysiological responses, and to determine whether these responses are modulated by sports-related concussion exposure in young male rugby athletes. METHODS: Nineteen male rugby athletes completed resting EEG recordings (eye-opened [EO] and eye-closed [EC]; 3 min each) and cognitive testing (Stroop, King-Devick) before and after cycling at ~75% age-predicted maximal heart rate (HR). Athletes were categorized as no history of SRC (N.=8) or multiple SRC (N.=11). Exercise-related changes in cognition and relative EEG power were analyzed using repeated-measures and mixed-model Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), with associations examined using Spearman's and partial correlations. RESULTS: Stroop scores increased, and King-Devick test completion time decreased following exercise (both P<0.001). Temporal beta and gamma power showed significant time effects (EC beta P=0.026; EC gamma P<0.001; EO gamma P=0.003; EO beta P=0.050). Occipital gamma power during EO demonstrated a significant time × group interaction (P=0.012). SRC burden was negatively associated with EO occipital gamma power change (r=-0.482, P=0.037), while EO temporal gamma change was associated with King-Devick test change after controlling for SRC exposure (r=0.494, P=0.037). CONCLUSIONS: Acute aerobic exercise was associated with improved cognition and modulation of resting-state EEG activity, while cumulative SRC exposure impaired exercise-induced cortical responsivity, particularly in EO occipital gamma responses.

item.title: White-matter microstructural alterations and cross-sectional thyroid hormone-cognition associations in hypothyroidism.
item.description:
European thyroid journal
PURPOSE: Hypothyroidism is associated with cognitive and emotional dysfunction, which may be accompanied by alterations in white-matter (WM) microstructure. However, few studies have compared diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures and clinical correlates across overt hypothyroidism (OH), subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH), and healthy controls (HCs). We investigated DTI-derived WM microstructural measures and their associations with thyroid function and neuropsychiatric performance in adult-onset hypothyroidism. METHODS: We enrolled 44 patients with OH, 41 with SCH, and 53 HCs. Thyroid function, neuropsychiatric assessments, and DTI data were collected. Age, sex, and years of education were entered simultaneously as covariates in all inferential group-comparison models, exploratory two-sided partial Spearman correlations, and exploratory cross-sectional indirect-effect models, except when these covariates themselves were the descriptive variables compared. RESULTS: Both OH and SCH groups had lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores and higher depression scores than HCs. Compared with SCH and HCs, the OH group showed more extensive between-group differences in DTI-derived metrics; no SCH-HC differences survived family-wise error correction. Within the OH group, DTI measures showed nominal, covariate-adjusted exploratory associations with thyroid hormone concentrations and neuropsychiatric scores. Exploratory covariate-adjusted models identified indirect associations of total triiodothyronine (TT3) and total thyroxine (TT4) with MoCA through fractional anisotropy (FA) of the left posterior thalamic radiation (PTR). The corresponding total and direct associations were not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, OH was associated with more extensive differences in DTI-derived WM measures than SCH. The exploratory indirect associations through left PTR FA do not establish a temporal or causal pathway.

item.title: Beyond Pathology: Perivascular Spaces as Dynamic Players in Neurodevelopment and Brain Health.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Perivascular spaces (PVS) have historically been viewed as radiological markers of aging and cerebrovascular pathology. However, this narrow perspective overlooks accumulating evidence that PVS likely undergo dynamic, prolonged maturation across the lifespan and may play an essential role in healthy brain development. This Viewpoint article challenges the prevailing paradigm by positioning PVS not as passive anatomical structures or mere disease indicators, but as active participants in postnatal neurodevelopment whose morphology and function evolve to meet the metabolic and waste clearance demands of the maturing brain. We integrate evidence from advanced neuroimaging, developmental neuroscience, and neurobiology studies to highlight that PVS structure and fluid dynamics may be coupled with several neurodevelopmental processes, impacted by early experiences, and mature through adolescence to facilitate healthy brain development and cognitive functioning. We advocate for longitudinal, lifespan approaches to PVS research, because understanding normative PVS development is paramount for interpreting pathological changes. This developmental reframing highlights new opportunities for early identification of at-risk individuals and preventive interventions targeting the brain's waste clearance system during sensitive developmental windows.

item.title: Mapping Individual Brain Deviations in ICD-11 Catatonia: Normative Modeling of Structural and Functional MRI Across Two Independent Cohorts.
item.description:
The American journal of psychiatry
Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome cutting across mood disorders (MODs) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). However, its neurobiological profiles remain poorly characterized. The authors examined structural and resting-state functional normative deviations associated with catatonia across two independent clinical cohorts, using hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling. Structural and resting-state functional MRI data were analyzed from two independent deeply phenotyped cohorts of 280 patients with MODs and SSDs. The Mannheim (Germany) sample included 184 patients with MODs or SSDs (58 with ICD-11 catatonia), and the Bern (Switzerland) sample comprised 96 SSD patients (59 with ICD-11 catatonia). Individual deviations from normative models were estimated using the PCNToolkit, based on healthy reference datasets (N=57,000 structural; N=22,000 functional). Catatonia diagnosis was associated with significant ventricular enlargement (third ventricle and left and right lateral ventricles; q<0.05) and cortical thinning in the left dorsal posterior cingulate and insular cortices (q<0.05) across both cohorts. Exploratory analyses identified a significant left orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) difference between MOD and SSD patients with catatonia. In the overall catatonia versus non-catatonia comparison, the OFC association survived false discovery rate correction only in models adjusted for demographic variables. Resting-state functional analyses showed reduced connectivity between sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and executive control networks at the nominal significance level, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. In the combined sample, catatonia was characterized by ventricular enlargement and cingulo-insular cortical thinning, supporting a transdiagnostic model implicating distributed motor-salience integration circuits. These findings provide reproducible, individual-level evidence for distributed brain network involvement in catatonia and identify candidate regions for future mechanistic and neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

item.title: Temporal confounds emulate multivariate fMRI measures of perceptual learning.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Any study of learning must capture neural or behavioural changes over time. Stimuli are therefore presented more than once, before and after learning takes place-a sequence that cannot be randomised across time. This design creates vulnerability to temporal confounds that cause illusory neural effects. We investigate this issue in a classic 'one-shot' learning paradigm, in which ambiguous two-tone images become recognisable after viewing a photo cue. Across common fMRI designs, we found that spurious correlations driven by the temporal proximity of stimuli created strong artefacts in multivariate data. Among certain experimental designs, we found strong neural markers of perceptual learning depending on how stimuli were distributed across these artefacts. This paradigm-dependent effect was present not only in the primary visual cortex (V1), but also in a non-visual control region (S1), indicative of an artefactual origin rather than a genuine perceptual learning effect. We present a principled approach to correct for this temporal order confound. Once applied, the artefactual learning signature was eliminated from both V1 and S1, and while the corrected signal retained information about image identity in V1, this was absent in S1. Our work demonstrates how current multivariate neuroimaging approaches to understanding learning could be influenced by methodological artefacts that misdirect interpretations towards distributed neural processing, and offers a practical framework to distinguish true learning from measurement error.

item.title: Distinct motor preparatory signals correlate with coarse vs fine control of self-paced action timing.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Making each action at the right time is crucial for motor control. In this study, we investigated how two prominent motor preparatory processes identified in human EEG-beta-band desynchronisation and the readiness potential (RP)-might each differently relate to the time of a simple voluntary action. In our paradigm, participants learned when to act in each block of trials, based on probabilistic trial-by-trial feedback. A reward schedule reinforced a specific optimal time to act in some blocks, but allowed greater variability around the same mean action time in other blocks. We found that contralateral motor beta-band power at the beginning of each trial was higher in trials with slow actions than in those with fast actions. In contrast, contralateral beta-band power reached stereotyped low values at the time of action, regardless of waiting times. Put together, this pattern is consistent with a neural implementation of distance-to-bound for a noisy accumulation process, in which baseline motor activity starts off closer to an action-triggering bound when fast actions are required. In turn, the RP was independent of the mean waiting time before action, but its slope increased when participants developed a precise motor plan. We suggest that beta desynchronisation and the RP track distinct, complementary processes involved in the temporal control of action. While beta-power activity at trial onset is consistent with a strategic adjustment of motor preparation to match the required pace of action, the modulation of the RP by motor plan precision is consistent with a temporally structured input to a ramping preparatory process. Simulations suggest that acting at the right time may involve increasing the strength of the input to this accumulator, which can drive the decision variable to drift towards the decision bound.

item.title: Healthy Sleep Mitigates the Association Between Cardiometabolic Disease and Poorer Cognitive and Brain Health.
item.description:
Journal of the American Heart Association
BACKGROUND: Cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and stroke, are important risk factors for dementia. We examined whether healthy sleep can support cognitive and brain health in people with CMDs. METHODS: The study included data from 408 977 adults from the UK Biobank. CMDs were defined using medical records, medication use, and medical history. Sleep patterns were defined using a composite score incorporating sleep duration, chronotype, insomnia symptoms, snoring, and daytime sleepiness. A subsample (n=34 913) underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging; volumes of total brain, gray matter, white matter, hippocampus, and white matter hyperintensities were ascertained. Associations of joint CMD (yes/no) and sleep (healthy, intermediate, poor) status with global and domain-specific cognitive scores and brain magnetic resonance imaging measures were examined using linear regression models. RESULTS: At baseline, 54017 (13.2%) participants had at least one CMD. In joint exposure analysis, performance in global cognition (β=0.02 [95% CI, 0.01-0.05]), verbal/numeric reasoning (β=0.07 [95% CI, 0.01-0.12]), and processing speed (β=0.07 [95% CI, 0.04-0.10]) was significantly higher among individuals with CMDs and a healthy sleep pattern, compared with those with CMDs and a poor sleep pattern. Similarly, in neuroimaging analyses, participants with CMDs and a healthy versus poor sleep pattern showed significantly larger total brain volume (β=0.22 [95% CI, 0.08-0.35]), gray matter volume (β=0.23 [95% CI, 0.09-0.36]), and white matter volume (β=0.19 [95% CI, 0.05-0.33]). CONCLUSIONS: Healthy sleep may attenuate the associations of CMDs with poorer cognitive performance and markers of brain atrophy. The findings highlight sleep as a modifiable factor that may support cognitive and brain health in individuals with CMDs.

item.title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease progression.
item.description:
Science advances
Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer's disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer's Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

item.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.
