item.title: Aggression in epilepsy and sleep: from historical accounts to brain networks and human behaviour.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
For a long time, epilepsy has been associated with violent behaviour, acquiring a highly stigmatizing reputation, shaped mainly by 19th century medical theories that postulated a direct connection between epilepsy and the criminal personality. Such stigma exerts a negative effect on the quality of life of people with epilepsy and remains a significant concern in forensic settings. This narrative review aims to provide a thorough exploration of the relationship between epilepsy and aggression, highlighting the misconceptions that contribute to this stigma. The evidence presented in this review draws on the authors' experience and a PubMed search conducted in December 2024. The manuscript is organized into five sections, addressing: (i) the historical and cultural background of epilepsy and violence; (ii) the clinical features of aggression as a peri-ictal manifestation; (iii) the neural networks underlying aggression in epilepsy; (iv) aggression in sleep-related disorders, an area closely related to epilepsy, where clinical interest and reports of sleep-related violent episodes have increased progressively in recent years; and (v) forensic considerations. In total, 326 records were identified through the PubMed search. Only papers relevant to the topics were included. Relevant publications were also added manually from the authors' own files. One hundred and thirty-two studies were ultimately included in this narrative review. The review, addressing the topic from a historical perspective, traces the evolution of stigma and the concept of the 'epileptic personality', from early observations to contemporary understanding. Next, we explore aggression and violence as peri-ictal manifestations, examining both their clinical characteristics and the brain networks implicated in the generation of aggressive behaviours during seizures. We try to elucidate the neurobiological substrates underlying these manifestations using intracerebral recordings. We then turn to violence associated with parasomnias, analysing and comparing the mechanisms underlying aggression and violence occurring in epileptic seizures with those observed during sleep in parasomnias, integrating evidence from intracranial EEG studies of disorders of arousal. This comparison highlights key similarities, differences and the risk of a misdiagnosis. Finally, we address the legal and forensic implications of seizure- and sleep-related aggression and violence. Epileptic seizures and parasomnias can cause injuries to the affected person or to those nearby, but they can rarely be truly classified as acts of violence. However, although aggressive behaviour is uncommon during seizures, it may lead to legal consequences. Despite efforts from scientific societies and patient organizations, the stigma of epilepsy persists, requiring further action and a deeper scientific understanding of this subject.

item.title: Dissociating executive prefrontal substrates following capsulotomy in obsessive-compulsive disorder.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by widespread executive function impairments linked to disrupted frontostriatal circuits. Ablative therapies such as capsulotomy show promising efficacy in treatment-refractory OCD, yet their effects on executive neural substrates remain poorly understood. This study explores how OCD and capsulotomy influence executive prefrontal function. Twenty-three post-capsulotomy OCD patients, 30 OCD controls and 32 health controls (HC) were recruited in the study. Post-capsulotomy patients were recruited at least 6 months following surgery to allow for postoperative stabilization. Participants completed three executive function tasks assessing distinct cognitive domains: the Extra-Dimensional Intra-Dimensional (EDID) task testing set-shifting, the N-back task testing working memory and the Flanker task measuring conflict processing. The EDID and N-back tasks were administered during concurrent task-based functional MRI, while the Flanker task provided only behavioural measures. In the EDID task, OCD capsulotomy patients demonstrated greater post-error flexibility towards ID versus ED shifting relative to both OCD controls and HC, despite exhibiting more ED errors. OCD controls showed less shifts after errors compared with HC, which was not revealed in the capsulotomy group. OCD patients showed less neural differentiation between ED versus ID in lateral and mesial prefrontal regions relative to HC. Capsulotomy was associated with decreased pre-supplementary motor area activity to ED shifts compared with HC, indicating impairments in neural reactivity to ED shifting. No evidence supported the influence of capsulotomy in the N-back or the Flanker tasks. Specifically, both OCD groups showed impaired working memory performance at high memory load along with dysfunction in the whole frontoparietal network. In the Flanker task, impairments in dissociating congruent and incongruent conditions were found in both OCD groups but not in the HC group. These findings suggest capsulotomy specifically remediates error-monitoring and behavioural flexibility through mesial prefrontal remodelling, while leaving working memory and conflict processing deficits intact. This dissociation implies that cognitive flexibility may represent a state-dependent process amenable to intervention, whereas working memory and conflict processing impairments may reflect trait markers of OCD vulnerability. These results have clinical implications on the relative safety profile of capsulotomy and patient selection for precision neuromodulation.

item.title: Blunted response of caudal locus coeruleus to arousing stimuli in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Parkinson's disease (PD) causes progressive degeneration of noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC), contributing to non-motor symptoms. Using neuromelanin-sensitive ultra-high field (7 T) MRI, we previously identified a reduction in neuromelanin signal in the caudal LC, indicating a rostro-caudal gradient of noradrenergic cell loss. Caudal LC degeneration was associated with greater severity of non-motor symptoms such as orthostatic hypotension and apathy. In the current case-control study, we expanded the PD cohort to further corroborate the structure-symptom relationships within the LC and investigate how degeneration along the rostro-caudal LC axis affects arousal-related functional responsivity. To this end, 71 people with PD in the ON-medication state and 40 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and 7 T magnetization transfer-weighted (MTw) MRI to quantify structural changes along the rostro-caudal LC axis. A subgroup of 30 people with PD and 27 controls underwent 7 T functional MRI to assess LC responsivity to arousing auditory and visual stimuli in two functional MRI sessions on separate days. Healthy controls were scanned twice without medication, while people with PD were studied on and off dopaminergic medication in counterbalanced order. In the PD group, MTw MRI confirmed a significant reduction of the regional neuromelanin signal in the caudal LC relative to the control group (P = 0.010). This structural disintegration correlated with orthostatic hypotension (P = 0.009) and cognitive impairment (P = 0.036), corroborating its clinical relevance. Functional MRI revealed reduced activation of the caudal LC to arousing visual and auditory stimuli in people with PD relative to controls (P = 0.012). This difference reached statistical significance only in the ON-medication state, with a similar but non-significant trend in the OFF-medication state (P = 0.105). In an exploratory analysis of a smaller subsample, structural and functional caudal LC signals were significantly correlated in both people with PD and healthy controls (P = 0.007). Together, the findings provide evidence for a rostro-caudal gradient of LC pathology in PD at both structural and functional levels. While structural MRI provides fine-grained insights into spatial gradients of disease-related pathology, functional MRI captures the impaired functional responsivity of the caudal LC. The presence of arousal-induced hypoactivation of the caudal LC in the ON-medication state indicates that LC dysfunction extends beyond dopamine deficits in PD, highlighting complex interactions between dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems.

item.title: Behavioural rigidity as a transdiagnostic marker of nucleus accumbens dysfunction in dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Behavioural rigidity, the tendency to persist with inflexible patterns of thoughts or actions, is increasingly recognized as a transdiagnostic symptom across psychiatric, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. Empirical studies exploring the prevalence and underlying neural mechanisms of behavioural rigidity in dementia, however, are lacking. This cross-sectional study sought to delineate the structural and functional neural correlates of behavioural rigidity using a transdiagnostic approach looking across the frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) spectrum and Alzheimer's disease (AD). A total of 204 participants were recruited, including 110 frontotemporal dementia (FTD), 53 AD and 41 healthy older control participants. Within the FTD group, 66 cases were diagnosed with clinically probable behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD), 26 presented with semantic dementia (SD) and 18 cases had progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA). Behavioural rigidity was assessed using the Stereotypical and Motor Behaviour subscale of the Cambridge Behavioural Inventory-Revised. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify grey matter regions associated with behavioural rigidity transdiagnostically, the results of which informed subsequent seed-based voxel-wise functional connectivity analyses. All imaging analyses were adjusted for relevant demographic and technical covariates. Statistical thresholds were set at voxel-level P < 0.001 (uncorrected) and cluster-level P < 0.05 (false discovery rate corrected). Our main finding was that behavioural rigidity is pervasive across dementia subtypes, ranging from most pronounced in bvFTD to milder/relatively absent in PNFA, relative to controls. Whole-brain VBM across the entire patient sample revealed a significant negative association between behavioural rigidity and grey matter intensity exclusively in the bilateral nucleus accumbens. Using the bilateral nucleus accumbens as seeds, resting-state functional connectivity analysis showed that higher levels of behavioural rigidity were associated with stronger connectivity between the left nucleus accumbens and the left supplementary motor area, paracentral lobule and precuneus. This is the first study, to our knowledge, to examine the neural substrates of behavioural rigidity across FTLD syndromes transdiagnostically using structural and functional neuroimaging approaches. Our findings reveal a gradation of rigid and repetitive behaviours, most apparent in bvFTD, which in turn reflects pathological disruption of the nucleus accumbens. Taken together, our findings highlight the need to consider repetitive and rigid behaviours as a transdiagnostic feature in neurodegenerative disorders, and one which indexes underlying nucleus accumbens pathology. More broadly, this study underscores the importance of screening for rigid and repetitive behaviours in the clinic and identifies the nucleus accumbens as a promising neural target to ameliorate these symptoms.

item.title: State-specific alterations in dynamic functional network connectivity in Wilson's disease: a resting-state fMRI study.
item.description:
Neurological research
BACKGROUND: Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) may reveal time-varying brain network abnormalities in Wilson's disease (WD) that are not captured by static analyses. We aimed to characterize static and dynamic large-scale network connectivity in WD using resting-state fMRI. METHODS: This retrospective study included 32 patients with WD and 32 healthy controls. Group independent component analysis identified eight components representing seven resting-state networks. Static connectivity was assessed across the full scan, while dynamic states were identified using sliding-window correlation and k-means clustering. State-specific connectivity and temporal metrics were compared between groups, and clinical associations were explored using Spearman correlation analyses. RESULTS: No sFNC difference survived false discovery rate correction. dFNC revealed group differences in States 2 and 4. In State 2, patients with WD showed increased default mode network (DMN)-left frontoparietal network connectivity and decreased DMN-dorsal attention network (DAN) and DMN-sensorimotor network connectivity. In State 4, DMN-left frontoparietal network and DAN-visual network connectivity increased, whereas DAN-right frontoparietal network connectivity decreased. Patients with WD also had shorter MDT in State 2, which correlated positively with blood urea nitrogen levels (Spearman's r = 0.478, FDR-corrected p = 0.035). CONCLUSION: WD showed state-specific changes in dynamic brain network connectivity that were not detected by static analysis. The correlation between State 2 MDT and blood urea nitrogen may reflect a relationship between brain network dynamics and peripheral metabolic status.

item.title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception.
item.description:
Nature neuroscience
Humans can swiftly learn to recognize visual objects after minimal exposure. Integrating new information with existing knowledge requires forming enduring neuronal representations to enable future recognition. Yet, the neuronal mechanisms in the human brain underlying such rapid perceptual changes remain unclear. Here we recorded single-neuron activity in occipital cortex (OC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions as participants rapidly learned to recognize degraded images. OC and MTL neurons modulated their activity to encode newly learned visual information and reshape perception. Population decoding revealed that OC neurons required additional processing time to resolve the identity of learned images, with delayed neuronal responses in the MTL. Our findings suggest that OC supports recognition after rapid learning via extensive recurrent processing, potentially involving higher-order neocortical areas, without relying on feedback from MTL. These results provide mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible models of visual recognition and few-shot visual learning.

item.title: Mapping cerebellar morphology in 15q11.2 CNV carriers using normative modeling.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Copy number variations (CNVs) at the 15q11.2 locus of the human genome have been associated with altered brain structure and increased risk for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. The cerebellum is increasingly seen as a crucial brain region for neurodevelopmental conditions, yet the effects of 15q11.2 CNVs on cerebellar morphology remain largely unclear. Importantly, 15q11.2 CNVs shows reduced or incomplete penetrance (meaning that not all CNV carriers are affected) and variable expressivity (meaning that symptoms may differ between individuals with the same genetic alteration). Thus, there is a need to not only assess group differences, but also to quantify anatomical variability at the individual level. Here, we address these issues using normative models of brain anatomy trained on large datasets (n > 52k, age range: 3-85) to assess both group and individual-level deviations in cerebellar anatomy in carriers of 15q11.2 deletions (n = 120, mean [SD] age = 64.95 [7.58]) and duplications (n = 149, mean [SD] age = 64.31 [7.21]), compared to non-carriers (n = 19,028, mean [SD] age = 64.31 [7.58]). Group-level case-control analyses revealed significantly smaller total and regional cerebellar volumes in both deletion and duplication carriers, though with small effect sizes. Individual-level deviation analyses, capturing pronounced alterations in specific individuals, revealed a heterogeneous pattern among carriers. Overall, our findings suggest that CNVs at the 15q11.2 locus exert modest and highly individualized effects on cerebellar morphology.

item.title: Neural connectomes of verbal fluency in post-stroke aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society : JINS
Verbal fluency tasks are widely used to assess language abilities and executive functions in both clinical and research settings. In post-stroke patients, prior research has indicated a significant hodological contribution to the neural basis of verbal fluency; however, this has largely been examined using lesion-based measures, predefined tractography approaches, and traditional diffusion metrics. Quantitative anisotropy-based structural connectometry derived from correlational tractography was employed to determine the white matter circuits underlying semantic and phonemic fluency in 44 patients with post-stroke aphasia. Both task types were found to be linked to anterior frontal connections of left-hemisphere dorsal and ventral associative pathways, as well as domain-general projection pathways. However, visual inspection of the connectomes, supported by supplementary cross-control analyses, suggested differences in the relative emphasis and distribution of pathways, with phonemic fluency aligning more with the dorsal stream, while semantic fluency showed greater reliance on the ventral stream and a wider range of cortico-subcortical connections. The findings contribute to current understanding of the neural networks of verbal fluency in aphasia, with potential relevance for clinical practice and research.

item.title: Motor Expertise Combines Lower Task Engagement with Enhanced Error Sensitivity.
item.description:
Cerebellum (London, England)
Skilled motor behaviour relies on complex predictive control and error processing. Despite its indispensable position in our everyday lives, neurobiological mechanisms of motor skill acquisition remain poorly understood. The presented study evaluates the functional dynamics and microstructural substrate of expertise-related reorganisation in predictive timing circuits using multimodal functional and quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. Forty-one baseball/softball players, representing a natural model of optimised motor timing programs, were compared against forty-six non-athletic controls using a structural connectome-informed hierarchical Bayesian framework jointly modelling task-based functional MRI dynamics of feedforward predictive control and error-driven modulation. Expertise-related microstructural differences were then characterised using neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging and adiabatic T₁ρ mapping. In non-athletic controls, predictive control was found to engage a distributed cortico-subcortical sensorimotor, visuospatial, attentional and frontoparietal loops, while higher-order associative systems were relatively down-regulated. However, quantitative deviation from the task optimum was associated with lower response across this predictive network. Expertise was characterised by higher behavioural performance but also by attenuated prediction-related functional engagement alongside enhanced error-related modulation. Furthermore, neurite density and orientation dispersion indices were higher in experts across distributed cortical networks, while the cerebellum exhibited a divergent profile characterised by higher neurite density, lower orientation dispersion and faster T₁ρ relaxation. These findings indicate that expertise involves lower task engagement within an established architecture despite higher behavioural performance, together with enhanced error sensitivity and distributed microstructural differences. This pattern is consistent with more efficient neural dynamics complemented with underlying tissue alterations.

item.title: Deciphering intratumoral heterogeneity: An interpretable radiopathologic framework for lymph node staging in early-stage cervical cancer.
item.description:
Medical oncology (Northwood, London, England)
Preoperative assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) informs treatment planning in early-stage cervical cancer (CC). Traditional radiomics (TR) may obscure intratumoral heterogeneity. We developed multiparametric MRI habitat radiomics (HR) for LNM prediction and explored its histopathologic context. Patients underwent radical surgery and lymphadenectomy. Part I comprised 148 training and 63 test patients; Part II comprised 14 for spatially matched histopathology. Intratumoral voxels were clustered into habitats by K-means using T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging (CE-T1WI) signals. The number of habitats was selected using validation AUC. HR/TR scores and clinical-radiological predictors were integrated by logistic regression. AUC and accuracy were compared by DeLong's and χ² tests. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) assessed contributions. Subregion-matched histopathology quantified Ki-67, CD3, CD31, and tumor-stroma ratio (TSR). LNM prevalence was 27.1% (61/225). The four-habitat HR model achieved a test AUC of 0.841 with 14 DWI/CE-T1WI-derived features. Test AUCs for clinical model (CL), TR, and HR + CL were 0.804, 0.784, and 0.890. HR + TR+CL achieved the highest AUC (0.902) and accuracy (87.30%), without a significant AUC difference from HR + CL (P = 0.277). SHAP ranked HR score above clinical lymph-node status, tumor diameter, and TR score. HR-3 exhibited highest Ki67 and lowest TSR, CD3, and CD31; HR-1 had highest TSR and lowest Ki67; HR-2 showed higher CD31 than HR-4. MRI-based HR may support preoperative LNM assessment in early-stage CC, with HR + CL representing a parsimonious candidate model for further evaluation. Spatially matched exploratory histopathology suggests possible regional tissue differences across MRI-defined habitats.

item.title: Network Reorganization of Right Precuneus Subregions Following Theta-Burst Stimulation.
item.description:
Brain topography
The precuneus is a heterogeneous posteromedial hub, but whether theta-burst stimulation (TBS) modulates its subregions differentially remains unclear. Here, we examined subregion-specific effects of intermittent TBS (iTBS) and continuous TBS (cTBS) applied to the right precuneus using structural MRI, resting-state functional MRI, and spectral dynamic causal modelling in 33 healthy adults scanned at baseline, post-iTBS, and post-cTBS. Three right precuneus subregions were defined as dorsal-anterior, dorsal-posterior, and ventral. Cortical thickness differed significantly across subregions, with greater thickness in the dorsal-anterior than in the dorsal-posterior and ventral precuneus. Whole-brain static functional connectivity showed significant main effects of condition and subregion, but no condition × subregion interaction. By contrast, dynamic functional connectivity revealed a significant condition × subregion interaction in the right orbital inferior frontal gyrus. Under iTBS, the ventral precuneus showed greater dynamic connectivity variability than the dorsal-anterior subregion, whereas under cTBS both dorsal subregions showed greater variability than the ventral subregion. Spectral dynamic causal modelling further demonstrated subregion-specific modulation of effective connectivity, with the most consistent between-region effects involving pathways to the left superior temporal gyrus and additional changes in self-connections. Baseline cortical thickness did not predict stimulation-induced changes in static or dynamic connectivity. These findings indicate baseline structural heterogeneity within the right precuneus and suggest that TBS related functional network reorganization differs across connectivity measures. Subregion-specific effects were most clearly expressed in dynamic and directed connectivity rather than uniformly across all connectivity measures. The results highlight the importance of subregion informed approaches for understanding and targeting precuneus centered networks.

item.title: Adolescent-onset spastic paraplegia associated with a TUBB4A p.Gly96Arg variant: insights from diffusion tensor tractography.
item.description:
Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
Adolescent-onset spastic paraplegia may present with heterogeneous underlying pathophysiology, including both axonal and myelin-related mechanisms. We report a 53-year-old woman with progressive spastic paraplegia beginning in adolescence who was found to harbor a pathogenic TUBB4A p.Gly96Arg variant. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse white-matter abnormalities and thinning of the corpus callosum, without basal ganglia or cerebellar atrophy, mimicking hereditary spastic paraplegia. Compared with three older healthy controls, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-based tractography showed lower fractional anisotropy and higher apparent diffusion coefficient across the corpus callosum, corticospinal tract, and middle cerebellar peduncle. Mean tract length was shorter in the corpus callosum but near the control means in the corticospinal tract and middle cerebellar peduncle, while streamline-count deviations also varied by tract. In this genetically confirmed case, DTI-based tractography provided supportive, hypothesis-generating characterization of white matter microstructural involvement. However, these observations do not establish an underlying pathological mechanism or an independent differential diagnostic role for DTI.
